abstract: The American dog tick, Dermacentor variabilis (Say), is found across most of the central and eastern portions of North America, and is a known vector of human and veterinary pathogens. While this tick has been found throughout this region for decades, there is still little understanding of the drivers for the highly variable annual densities. To explore the relative effects of hosts, environmental conditions, and tick biology, we introduce ADTSIM 2.0, an upgraded version of the ADTSIM model that simulates the lifecycle of D. variabilis. The model uses a weekly time step and follows the life stages (egg, larvae, nymph, and adult), questing behavior, host-seeking dynamics, and survival rates under varying environmental conditions. The model includes calculations for tick interactions with small- and medium-sized mammal hosts and factors in critical environmental influences such as temperature on tick development and questing activity. It addresses the effect of questing behavior on tick longevity, emphasizing the trade off between survival and host-seeking. The results show that accurate estimates of both host densities and weather information are critical to predict local D. variabilis densities. This model provides the first step to building a tool for public health information, offering a framework for assessing tick control measures and is adaptable to add tick-borne pathogen dynamics for both human and animal diseases.
